lesson_text: Where buyers tend to stop a fall. That's support. Each time price came down there, enough buyers showed up to turn it. You find support at the earlier lows where the stock turned back up. It doesn't have to be the lowest price ever. It's a floor, and floors break. So treat it as a place to put your stop just under, not a promise that the stock holds. Support is a floor made of buyers. Floors break, so your stop goes under it.

depth.summary: A long lower shadow means sellers drove price lower during the session. Buyers then bid price back up by the close, which leaves the long lower shadow. A small body near the top of the bar means buyers took control by the end. A shooting star does not guarantee a reversal. Don't act on a candle pattern until it has formed and a breakout activates it. A candlestick needs the open, high, low and close for each period. A candle shows the open, close, high and low for its period.

reveal_json.lesson_line: A long lower wick shows where buyers showed up. It describes today, it doesn't promise tomorrow.

depth.summary: A symmetrical triangle has a falling upper line and a rising lower line that converge. Bulkowski: symmetrical triangle, bottom line up, top line down. Fidelity's guide: symmetrical triangle, falling upper line, rising lower line. An ascending triangle has a flat upper line and a rising lower line. Bulkowski: a rectangle has flat tops and flat bottoms between two parallel lines. A rising wedge sits between two up-sloping lines that converge. Unlike the neutral symmetrical triangle, the rising wedge slopes up and carries a bearish bias. A descending triangle has a flat lower line and a falling upper line. Fidelity's guide: a wedge's two lines point the same way, with at least five touches, three on one line and two on the other.

They don't point the same way either, so it's not a wedge. This one has no lean. The break sets the direction, so you wait for it.

wrong.Rising wedge: In a wedge both lines slope the same way. Here they point opposite ways.

lesson_text: Half to three-quarters of the way in. Measure from where the lines start to the apex. A break before halfway can be early and fail. A break right at the apex means little, because the range is used up. In one big study the breaks came about 74% of the way in, right in that zone. I don't trade off this ratio. It just tells you a triangle that drifts into its point has run out of room. Good triangle breaks come before the apex, not at it.

If the $30 floor breaks, you just stay away. Let the breakout pick the direction. The textbook lean doesn't.

depth.summary: A drawdown is the percent fall from a peak to the low after it. A drawdown runs from a peak to the next valley. A drawdown is a fall in account value, from closed losses or open ones. A drawdown is not always a loss. A retirement drawdown means withdrawals; a market drawdown means a fall in value. Drawdown is measured from the peak, while a loss is measured from what you paid.

reveal_json.simple: It's the drop from the account's peak to its low, measured from the high, not from what you put in.
reveal_json.why: The drop from the peak to the low. You measure from the high, not from where you started. It counts open losses too, not just closed trades. So you can be in a drawdown and still be up overall. Watch it, because our size steps down as the drawdown grows.

wrong.Your loss below what you put in: A drawdown runs from the peak. You can be in one and still be in profit.

lesson_text: Losses too big to come back from. Ruin is the account getting so small it can't trade its way back. It doesn't have to mean zero. It's whatever drawdown would make you quit. Big size per trade plus a normal losing run is how you get there. Small risk per trade keeps you in the game. Survival comes first. An edge is worthless once the account can't trade it.

lesson_text: Slowing its bond buying, then ending it. In November 2021 the Fed announced it would phase out its purchases. In December it doubled the pace, with buying set to end by mid-March 2022. A taper doesn't shrink what the Fed owns. It just adds less each month until it stops. Shrinking the pile is QT, and that came later. Watch the words too: in 2013 a hint of a taper alone sent yields spiking. Taper is QE winding down, not QT. The Fed stops adding before it starts shrinking.

answer_json.answer: How many stocks join the index's move

lesson_text: Most stocks joined the index's move. That's all breadth is: how many stocks took part. It's not how far the index went or how fast. An index can rise on a handful of giants. Breadth tells you whether the rest of the market came along. I want to know that before I press, because a move most stocks join has more under it. Don't mix it up with market depth. That's how big an order trades without moving the price. The index tells you where. Breadth tells you how many came along.

lesson_text: A few positions, then more as they work. The first Green day after a correction can be a head fake. Buy a full book, it fails, and every stop hits at once. Start with a few of your best setups. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you add more positions. If they fail, you lost a little and you're still mostly in cash. Each trade goes on at full size, at one price, with one stop. Let the market earn your exposure. After a correction, ease back in: a few positions first, more only as they work.

lesson_text: Let it go and wait for a new setup. At 15% over the buy point, the entry you planned is gone. We don't buy more than 4% above the buy point. Past that you're chasing, and chasing costs you size. Your stop still belongs under the buy point, so the gap to it gets wide and your share count shrinks. A late entry can also land right when the move is ready to pull back. The stock may keep going, and that's fine. It's just not your trade anymore. There's always another setup. Wait for one you can plan.

Fear of missing a move is FOMO. Holding a loser too long is the disposition effect. Tilt is anger. It builds a little after each stop-out until one bad decision turns into five. Catch it early. Once you feel it, you're done with new trades for the day. Tilt is anger placing your trades. Spot it early and step away.

answer_json.answer: Thinking a streak is 'due' to end

lesson_text: Thinking a streak is 'due' to end. After three heads in a row, the believer is sure tails is coming. The coin doesn't remember. The hot hand is the flip side, believing the run will keep going. In trading it sounds like 'I've lost four in a row, the next one has to work.' It doesn't have to. The next trade doesn't know about the last few. Take it or skip it on its own merits. The next trade doesn't know about the last few.

lesson_text: Gambler's fallacy. Five losses don't make a win due. Trades aren't coin flips, but nothing about a losing run loads the next one in your favor. A streak can be plain bad luck. It can also mean something changed, in the market or in how you're trading the setup. Doubling size on a hunch fixes neither. We don't have a losing-streak rule. Size comes down only through the drawdown ladder, which tracks how far the account sits below its high. So check the five trades, and keep the size where your rules put it. Never size up because a win feels due. Size follows your rules, not the streak.

answer_json.answer: Judging a choice by how it turned out

lesson_text: Judging a choice by how it turned out. You broke your plan and got paid, so it feels smart. It wasn't. Good decisions can lose, and bad ones can win. Grade the decision and the result separately. Follow every rule and get stopped out, and that's a good trade. Ignore your stop and get lucky, and that's a bad one. It's the dangerous kind too, because it teaches you to do it again. Grade the decision and the result separately. They're two different grades.

So step back and figure out if it's the market or how you're running it. Sitting it out while it's choppy is fine. Throwing it out is too much. Sizing up to win it back is how a bad two weeks becomes a bad year. A play that fits one market can sit out the next. Review it, don't force it.

lesson_text: Paper trading. Fake money, live market data, and the orders never reach a real exchange. It's a good way to learn your platform and your routine without risking a dollar. Just know it proves less than real trades do. A backtest runs rules over past data instead. Swing trading and day trading are styles, about how long you hold. Paper trading is practice. It costs nothing, and it proves less than real trades.

lesson_text: The same day. We journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally. By month end you won't remember what you were thinking on Tuesday. Or how it felt when it moved against you. Those notes are the whole point. The broker logs the fills. Only you can log why you took it. Then each month we review the numbers, like win rate and expectancy. Ideally, journal each trade the same day and review the week each weekend.
